Table 9: Per-intent accuracy (%) for all seven models on the 662 valid samples. Sample counts: product search 83, knowledge reasoning 106, rating quality 80, feature combination 104, negative constraint 57, use-case scenario 104, coupon budget 33, review-driven 95.

Table 8: Interaction behavior mined from trajectories: mean calls to key tools, the relative position of the first ask_user (0=start, 1=end), and the finish rate. Two styles emerge—deep-search/late-ask (Opus, Kimi, MiniMax) versus shallow-search/early-ask (GPT family).
Table 6: Core statistics of the current EComAgentBench benchmark, computed from the current benchmark release.

Table 1: EComAgentBench versus recent e-commerce shopping benchmarks, grouped by its three goals: explaining failures (RQ1), realistic hidden intent (RQ2), and a reliable, automated build (RQ3). EComAgentBench is the only one that meets all three; each prior benchmark already misses at least one capability in the reliability group (ShoppingBench has no task validation, ShopSimulator is hand-annotated, DeepPlanning uses synthetic products).
Table 10: Abridged correct trajectory for a representative review-driven sample under gpt-5.4.

Figure 1: EComAgentBench on one task (wireless charger). Top: (a) the full requirement is split across three sources: a visible query with implicit cues, a hidden persona behind get_user_profile, and hidden clarification behind ask_user; (b) the agent interacts with the shopper and a sandboxed shop to recover them; (c) the recommended product is graded against typed rubrics tagged by source (a case is correct on exact product match or full rubric satisfaction). Bottom: an abridged trajectory of the recovery. Source colors (query in blue, persona in orange, clarification in green) carry across panels.

Figure 4: Interaction style versus accuracy. Early-ask models (GPT family) cluster on the left; late-ask, deepsearch models (Opus, Kimi, MiniMax) on the right. Marker size encodes search depth. No single style dominates—the best accuracy (Opus) pairs deep search with late clarification.

Figure 3: (a) Hidden sources (persona, clarification) stay harder than query-visible constraints. (b) The number of implicitly stated query requirements is a stronger difficulty driver than raw rubric count.
